connection: Production contains Employee, Address, and ClockEntry. This session keeps its record-equality experiment in ScratchPad as Session10WorkSummary, so it does not pre-create the production WorkSummary report type introduced in Session 22.
objectives: Predict, and then confirm, that two separately-constructed ClockEntry objects with identical EmployeeId/ClockIn/Clockout are NOT equal by default -- neither ClockEntry nor Employee overrides Equals.
Confirm that two Session10WorkSummary records with the same EmployeeId and Hours ARE equal, because record types generate value-based equality automatically.
Explain why EmployeeDirectory's city-uniqueness check uses StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase rather than default string equality.
Distinguish struct value-copy semantics (WorkCode, a record struct) from class reference semantics (ClockEntry, Employee).

visuals.title: class gives you reference equality unless you opt out
visuals.explanation: new ClockEntry(1, t) != new ClockEntry(1, t) is true (they are unequal) -- ClockEntry never overrode Equals, so two separately-constructed objects are never equal, even with identical field values.

visuals.title: record gives you value equality automatically
visuals.explanation: new Session10WorkSummary(1, 8m) == new Session10WorkSummary(1, 8m) is true -- the compiler generates Equals/GetHashCode from the record's declared members.

visuals.title: Case sensitivity is a choice, not a default
visuals.explanation: "Springfield" == "springfield" is false under ordinal string comparison; EmployeeDirectory explicitly opts into StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase to treat them as the same city.

visuals.title: record struct copies by value, like int or DateTime
visuals.explanation: WorkCode is declared readonly record struct -- assigning one WorkCode variable to another copies its Year and Sequence, the same as any other value type.

Yes -- it compares EmployeeId, ClockIn, and Clockout
Yes, but only Clockout is compared
preQuiz.explanation: Nothing in the real ClockEntry.cs overrides Equals or GetHashCode -- confirmed by reading the actual file; it relies entirely on object identity.

preQuiz.prompt: Why does new Session10WorkSummary(1, 8m).Equals(new Session10WorkSummary(1, 8m)) return true without any equality code written for it?
options: Session10WorkSummary is declared as a record, and the compiler automatically generates member-wise Equals/GetHashCode/== for records
decimal always compares by value across all types
Session10WorkSummary happens to be a singleton
preQuiz.explanation: record is a C# feature specifically for value-equality-by-default types -- Session10WorkSummary gets this for free from its declaration, unlike the plain class ClockEntry.

preQuiz.prompt: What would "Springfield" == "springfield" evaluate to using C#'s default string equality?
options: false -- default string comparison is ordinal (case-sensitive) unless you explicitly choose a case-insensitive comparer
preQuiz.explanation: C#'s default == for string is ordinal and case-sensitive; EmployeeDirectory has to opt into StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase specifically to treat differently-cased city names as duplicates.

concept.title: ClockEntry and Employee: reference equality, by default and by choice
paragraphs: ClockEntry and Employee are both plain class declarations with no Equals override anywhere in the production code. That means == and .Equals() compare object identity: are these two variables pointing at the very same object?
This is a real, verified fact about the actual repository, not an assumption -- reading Models/ClockEntry.cs and Models/Employee.cs directly confirms neither type overrides equality members.

concept.title: A ScratchPad record gets value equality automatically
paragraphs: public sealed record Session10WorkSummary(int EmployeeId, decimal Hours) is a positional record. Declaring it with record instead of class is what generates member-wise Equals, GetHashCode, and == overloads -- no extra code required.

The sealed keyword means another type cannot inherit from Session10WorkSummary. It is not an access modifier, and it is not responsible for the generated equality. public controls where the record can be used, sealed prevents inheritance, and record supplies the value-based record behavior. Session10WorkSummary is sealed because it is intended to be a complete result type rather than a base type for other records.
This is the real, meaningful contrast this session teaches: the same 'compare these two objects' question gets a different default answer depending on whether the type is declared class or record.

concept.title: String comparison is a choice you make explicitly
paragraphs: For now, think of HashSet<T> as a collection that keeps each value only once. If you add a value it already considers equal to an existing value, it does not add a duplicate. You will learn HashSet<T> in more detail in Session 12.
EmployeeDirectory's Cities set is constructed with new HashSet<string>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase) specifically so "Springfield" and "springfield" collapse into one entry.

Without that explicit comparer, HashSet<string>'s default ordinal comparison would treat them as two different cities -- exactly the kind of silent data-quality bug case-insensitive matching exists to prevent.

postQuiz.prompt: If ClockEntry were changed to a record instead of a class, what would change about existing code that stores ClockEntry objects in a List and looks them up by reference?
options: Value equality would mean two field-identical ClockEntry objects become interchangeable for Equals-based lookups, which could silently change behavior anywhere identity currently mattered (like GetClockEntry's FirstOrDefault)
Nothing would change -- record and class behave identically
The code would fail to compile
postQuiz.explanation: Switching class to record is not a purely cosmetic change -- it changes the equality semantics every consumer of that type relies on, which is exactly why this session treats it as a real design decision, not a syntax preference.

postQuiz.prompt: Why is WorkCode declared as a readonly record struct instead of a record (class)?
options: record struct combines record's generated value equality with struct's copy-by-value semantics -- appropriate for a small, immutable value like a year+sequence pair
record struct is required syntax for any type with two properties
There is no difference between record and record struct
postQuiz.explanation: record struct is specifically for small, copyable, value-equality types -- exactly what a WorkCode(Year, Sequence) pair is.

postQuiz.prompt: Would GetEmployeeClockEntries's real Where filter (entry.EmployeeId == employeeId) behave any differently if ClockEntry had record value equality instead of reference equality?
options: No -- that filter compares an int (EmployeeId) to an int, which already uses value equality regardless of whether ClockEntry itself is a class or record
Yes -- it would start matching by full object equality instead
postQuiz.explanation: The filter never compares whole ClockEntry objects to each other -- it compares one of their int fields, which is unaffected by ClockEntry's own equality semantics.

reflections.question: Why might a real codebase deliberately choose reference equality for ClockEntry rather than adding value equality?
reflections.answer: A ClockEntry can represent one specific business event with its own identity and lifecycle. Two entries may coincidentally share EmployeeId and ClockIn while still being distinct records, and Clockout can change later. Reference equality preserves that distinction unless the domain explicitly defines a stable value-based identity.

reflections.question: What would you need to add to ClockEntry to make two field-identical instances equal, and what would you risk changing by doing so?
reflections.answer: You would define value equality by overriding Equals and GetHashCode and normally == and !=, or redesign ClockEntry as a record. You must choose the participating members and keep their hash behavior stable. Otherwise, distinct events could collapse in a HashSet or compare equal unexpectedly, and mutating an equality member after dictionary insertion could make the object difficult to find.

reflections.question: Where else in this codebase might case-insensitive string comparison matter, beyond EmployeeDirectory's city set?
reflections.answer: It could matter for user-entered employee-name searches, email-like identifiers, external codes, or other text whose business meaning ignores letter case. It should not be applied automatically: passwords, case-sensitive external identifiers, and display text can require different rules. The domain requirement should choose the comparer explicitly.

whatBreaks: Assuming ClockEntry has value equality would lead to bugs anywhere code tries to deduplicate or compare ClockEntry objects by field value instead of by reference. Changing Session10WorkSummary from record to class would change this ScratchPad comparison from value equality to reference equality. Removing EmployeeDirectory's StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase would let differently-cased city names silently multiply instead of being treated as one city.
summary: class gives you reference equality unless you explicitly override it, while record gives you value equality automatically. Session10WorkSummary demonstrates that contrast in ScratchPad without claiming Session 22's production WorkSummary name early. String comparison remains an explicit domain choice.
